question: A 23-year-old man comes to the physician with a 1-week history of sharp, substernal chest pain that is worse with inspiration and relieved with leaning forward. He has also had nausea and myalgias. His father has coronary artery disease. His temperature is 37.3°C (99.1°F), pulse is 110/min, and blood pressure is 130/84 mm Hg. Cardiac examination shows a high-pitched rubbing sound between S1 and S2 that is best heard at the left sternal border. An ECG shows depressed PR interval and diffuse ST elevations. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient’s symptoms?
reasoning_chain: CHAIN: "Sharp substernal chest pain" -> "worse with inspiration" -> "relieved by leaning forward" -> "suggestive of pericarditis" -> "high-pitched rubbing sound" -> "indicates pericardial friction rub" -> "ECG shows diffuse ST elevations" -> "consistent with acute viral infection" -> 85%

CHAIN: "Substernal chest pain" -> "nausea and myalgias" -> "fever of 37.3°C" -> "high pulse rate of 110/min" -> "pericardial friction rub present" -> "depressed PR interval on ECG" -> "indicates inflammation of the pericardium" -> "most likely due to acute viral infection" -> 90%

CHAIN: "Patient has chest pain" -> "family history of coronary artery disease" -> "but young age reduces likelihood of myocardial infarction" -> "symptoms suggest pericarditis" -> "high-pitched rubbing sound" -> "ECG findings support viral etiology" -> "most likely cause is acute viral infection" -> 80%

CHAIN: "Chest pain with inspiration" -> "relieved by leaning forward" -> "suggests pericarditis" -> "presence of friction rub" -> "ECG shows ST elevations" -> "common in viral infections" -> "less likely to be Dressler syndrome due to timing" -> "most likely cause is acute viral infection" -> 75%
analysis: The patient's symptoms, including sharp substernal chest pain that worsens with inspiration and is relieved by leaning forward, along with the presence of a pericardial friction rub and ECG findings of diffuse ST elevations and depressed PR interval, are indicative of acute pericarditis. The most common cause of acute pericarditis in young adults is often viral infections. Given the context and the age of the patient, an acute viral infection is the most likely cause of his symptoms.
